content: Transcellular fluid is the smallest component of extracellular fluid, which also includes interstitial fluid and plasma. It accounts for approximately 5% of the total body water. Examples of transcellular fluid include gastrointestinal fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, ocular fluid, synovial (joint) fluid, and urine stored in the bladder. The composition of transcellular fluid varies significantly depending on its location within the body. Some of the electrolytes commonly found in transcellular fluid include sodium ions, chloride ions, and bicarbonate ions. Transcellular fluid serves diverse physiological functions. In the joints, it acts as a lubricant, facilitating smooth movement. In the case of urine, it plays a critical role in the excretion of electrolytes and other molecules from the body.
